question: to the Commission Alessandro Ciriani (ECR) Subject:

For years, residents of Montesanto and the northern part of Gorizia, near the border with Solkan (Nova Gorica), have been reporting unpleasant odours and serious environmental issues caused by the Livarna Gorica foundry, located close to the Italian border in Slovenia. According to ARPA FVG (Friuli Venezia Giulia Regional Environmental Protection Agency), the reports of odours have increased significantly since May 2025 and their nature suggests that they are emanating from the foundry’s activities. In all, 140 reports were registered in September 2025, 96 in November 2025, 109 in February 2026 and 93 in March 2026, with a high proportion coming from the Montesanto area. This issue has a clear cross-border dynamic and may require action to verify compliance with Directive 2010/75/EU on industrial emissions, with best available techniques and with requirements for Member States to cooperate with one another. In view of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of this situation and does it intend to ask the competent Slovenian authorities for further information?
Does it consider it necessary to verify whether the plant is operating in line with Directive 2010/75/EU and the relevant best available techniques (BAT)?
Will it promote stable and transparent cross-border monitoring of air quality in the Gorizia-Nova Gorica area?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.7.2026) The Commission is aware of cross-border odour emissions from the industrial facility Livarna Gorica d.o.o and understands that exchanges have been initiated between Italian and Slovenian local authorities. The Commission therefore does not intend to intervene at this stage. In its role as guardian of the Treaties, the Commission monitors the application of EU law and may decide to take appropriate action, in line with its enforcement priorities1. On 6 December 2024, Commission implementing decision on Best Available Techniques conclusions for the smitheries and foundries industry2 was published and permits of existing installations must be updated within four years to comply with these norms, including on odour. In addition, Article 26 of the Industrial Emissions Directive3 requires cooperation between neighbouring Member States to limit the consequences for the environment and human health of installations’ operations. This includes consultation of the other Member State during the permitting procedure. Under the Air Quality Directive4, where exceedances of air quality limit or target values are significantly affected by pollution transported from another Member State, Member States should notify the Commission and cooperate with concerned Member States to address the exceedances. Based on the latest available data reported to the Commission – for 2024 – there have been no exceedances of air quality standards in Gorizia nor Nova Gorica for particulate matter, nitrogen dioxide or benzo(a)pyrene.
1 Communication from the Commission - EU law: Better results through better application, OJ C 18, 19.1.2017,

p. 10–20, and Communication from the Commission - Enforcing EU law for a Europe that delivers, 13.10.2022, COM(2022) 518 final. 2 Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2024/2974 establishing the best available techniques (BAT) conclusions under the Industrial Emissions Directive for the smitheries and foundries industry: https://eurlex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02024D2974-20241206. 3 Directive (EU) 2024/1785 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 April 2024 amending Directive 2010/75/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council on industrial emissions (integrated pollution prevention and control) and Council Directive 1999/31/EC on the landfill of waste, OJ L, 2024/1785, 15.7.2024. 4 Article 21 of Directive (EU) 2024/2881 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2024 on ambient air quality and cleaner air for Europe (recast), OJ L, 2024/2881, 20.11.2024.
